title: Disaster recovery money can enter a place without agencies knowing whether local firms received the work
source_unit: U.S. Government Accountability Office GAO-26-108426 review of FEMA and Army Corps disaster contracting after Hurricane Helene, Maui wildfires, and Hurricane Ian
geography: Declared disaster areas associated with Hurricane Helene, the Maui wildfires, and Hurricane Ian

observations.period: Selected disasters and contracts reviewed through 2026

denominator.unit: nongeneralizable selected FEMA and Army Corps post-disaster contracts

disasters_reviewed.unit: Hurricane Helene, Maui wildfires, and Hurricane Ian

fema_contract_sample.value: 25 contracts: 12 local-vendor awards and 13 nonlocal-vendor awards

corps_contract_sample.value: 15 contracts: 7 local-vendor awards and 8 nonlocal-vendor awards

fema_recorded_local_share.unit: percent of $2.9 billion in FEMA contract obligations identified in agency data as local-vendor contracts; approximately $85 million

local_area_identification_error.unit: of 13 contracting officers who awarded local-vendor contracts and incorrectly identified the local disaster area

corps_documentation.value: all selected Corps contracts lacked documents related to local-vendor use

local_economic_recovery.unit: local jobs, wages, business survival, subcontracting, project quality, and household recovery

observations.method: GAO review of law, regulation, policy, agency tracking sheets, interviews with officials and contracting officers, and a nongeneralizable sample of 40 contracts from three selected disasters.
observations.uncertainty: The FEMA 3% figure describes the recorded local-vendor field for three selected disasters and may reflect coding, monitoring, local capacity, advance contracts, or actual award patterns. The contract sample cannot support a national rate or causal local-economic effect.
observations.subgroup: FEMA and Army Corps disaster contracts and contracting officers associated with Hurricane Helene, the Maui wildfires, and Hurricane Ian; local and nonlocal vendors are separate award categories.
observations.counterinterpretation: Nonlocal vendors may be necessary when disaster-area firms lack capacity, supplies, speed, or functioning infrastructure; the statutory local preference applies only when feasible and practicable, so a low recorded local share is not by itself proof of wrongdoing or poor response.

related_sources.claim: Federal Acquisition Regulation local-area preference requires preference for local firms to the extent feasible and practicable in covered disaster contracts.

boundary: This record captures disaster-contracting policy, selected contracts, recorded local-vendor share, and agency monitoring gaps. It does not establish a national local-vendor rate, contract quality, local jobs or business survival, household recovery, agency wrongdoing, or causal economic impact.
